name: Narrow palate theory

lead: The narrow palate theory holds that the width and shape of the roof of the mouth shapes the face above it. Proponents say a narrow, high-arched palate goes with a recessed maxilla, narrow dental arch, buccal corridors and less support for the cheeks and under-eyes, and that widening the palate is a way to improve midface appearance.

Orthodontic literature does recognise narrow upper arches as a common transverse discrepancy and treats them with expanders. Whether expansion changes facial aesthetics beyond the teeth and airway, and how much a narrow palate contributes to overall looks, is discussed far more in forums than in published research.

paras: In practice people compare their palate with others in photos, look at smile width and buccal corridors, and ask orthodontists about expansion. Options discussed range from rapid palatal expanders in younger patients to mini-implant-assisted expansion (MARPE/MSE) and surgically assisted expansion in adults, usually alongside braces. Some also discuss tongue posture.

Expansion appliances can cause speech changes, extra saliva, soreness, gaps between front teeth and relapse; adult techniques add mini-implant or surgical risks. Orthodontists and oral surgeons assess whether a transverse deficiency actually exists before treatment.

angle.text: Followers of the theory try to widen the upper arch, most commonly with expanders, to improve smile width and midface support. How far the face changes beyond the teeth is the part that is disputed.

lead: The narrow palate theory is a looksmaxxing framework linking the width and vault height of the hard palate to facial development. In its common form it says a narrow, high-arched palate accompanies a recessed or underdeveloped maxilla, a narrow nasal floor and crowded teeth, and that these show up as flatter cheeks, hollow under-eyes, visible buccal corridors and a less forward midface.[1][2]

People who hold this view use it to explain why some faces look less supported and as a reason to consider palatal expansion, oral posture work and related jaw procedures, with the aim of a wider smile, more midface support and more room for the tongue. Others on the same forums argue that palate width is a minor factor next to teeth, gums and bone structure, and point to people with narrow palates who are widely regarded as attractive.[1][2]

Orthodontic literature treats a narrow maxillary arch as a common transverse problem and describes a narrow palate among the dental findings in some people with obstructive sleep apnea.[3][4] The idea draws on the older orthotropics tradition of John and Mike Mew, who argued that tongue posture shapes the upper jaw.[5] Claims about the effect of palate width on overall facial attractiveness have not been tested in clinical trials.

paras: The hard palate is the bony roof of the mouth and the floor of the nasal cavity, formed by the maxilla and the palatine bones; it separates the mouth from the nasal passages and works with the tongue in speech and feeding.[6] A high-arched or narrow palate is one that is unusually vaulted or narrow compared with population averages. It can occur alone or alongside various genetic syndromes, and often comes with crowded teeth and a narrow nasal airway.[7]

Clinicians describe the vault with measurements such as palatal height and a palatal vault index (height divided by width). Reference material gives normal adult vault height of roughly 15 to 16 mm, with indexes above about 50 to 60 described as high-arched.[7]

In looksmaxxing discussion the term usually means a narrow upper arch and recessed maxilla seen together with a narrow smile and visible buccal corridors, the dark spaces at the corners of the smile. Members compare palates in photos and ask how to tell whether they have one.[1]

The theory's roots lie in orthotropics, developed by British orthodontist John Mew (1928-2025) and carried on by his son Mike Mew. John Mew argued that the resting posture of the tongue exerts an outward force that widens the upper jaw in growing children and keeps the maxilla from growing downward and backward, and he combined palatal expanders, diet change and tongue training in his approach.[5]

Mainstream orthodontists opposed his views on the causes of malocclusion, and a 2019 article in the Journal of Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery concluded the evidence for orthotropic treatment is inadequate, as summarised on Wikipedia.[5] Interest in the associated 'mewing' posture technique rose from 2019 and spread on social media, including looksmaxxing communities.[8] Within those communities, palate width became one of the structural markers discussed alongside the maxilla, cheekbones and jaw.[2]

Proponents describe palate width as a marker of how well the midface developed. One forum participant writes that a wide palate is a sign of good facial development, alongside high cheekbones and a forward maxilla.[2] Others say narrow palates often come with a narrow nasal cavity and crowding, but not always.[1]

Some members connect palate width to oral posture and mouth breathing, arguing that too little oral volume makes proper tongue posture hard, and discuss pairing expansion with other jaw work.[9] A thread on the topic describes plans to use testosterone and a growth-hormone secretagogue with the aim of bone growth in someone with a narrow palate.[9]

A thread arguing that MSE and MARPE are less effective than multisegment bimaxillary surgery shows the community itself disagrees on the best fix.[10] Another thread compares MSE with segmental Le Fort surgery for narrow arches and nasal breathing.[11] Teenagers also post about planning braces plus MSE or a palatal expander because of a narrow palate.[12]

Reference material lists genetic and syndromic associations, such as Marfan, Ehlers-Danlos, Noonan, Stickler and Down syndromes, and non-genetic contributors such as prolonged thumb-sucking or pacifier use, chronic mouth breathing from allergy or adenoid enlargement, and tongue-tie.[7] A meta-analysis on pacifiers reported that use beyond about age 3 was associated with posterior crossbite, narrower upper intercuspid width and a high narrow palate, and that habits stopped by age 2 to 3 did not alter the dentition.[13]

The Wikipedia article on mouth breathing says chronic mouth breathing in children may affect dental and facial growth and may lead to a long, narrow face, while noting the reverse direction is also proposed and that the health impact is an active area of orthodontic research.[14]

Palatal expanders widen the upper arch so the upper and lower teeth fit together. They are most common at ages 8 to 18; in adults expansion is slower and more uncomfortable, and braces usually follow. Wikipedia lists indications such as an upper jaw at least 4 mm narrower than the lower, cleft palate repair, moderate crowding and airway expansion.[15]

Rapid palatal expansion uses a screw turned daily to separate the midpalatal suture, then a retention period of several months. Slow expansion works over weeks. MARPE (mini-implant assisted) anchors the appliance in the palate so force reaches bone and can expand young adults whose suture has fused, though many adults may still need surgical help; SARPE adds a surgical cut for mature palates.[15] Reference material reports about 4 to 6 mm of posterior expansion with MARPE and about 6 mm with SARPE.[7]

Orthognathic options such as Le Fort I or maxillomandibular advancement are discussed for airway and facial reasons.[7] Conservative approaches include habit cessation, orofacial myofunctional therapy and allergy management.[7] In looksmaxxing forums, members compare expansion with jaw surgery, often alongside braces.[10][11]

A 2023 review describes transverse maxillary deficiency as the most common discrepancy orthodontists face, with a narrow palate and posterior crossbite among its manifestations, and covers slow, rapid and surgically assisted expansion.[3] A review of sleep apnea and mandibular advancement devices lists a narrow palate among dental and orofacial signs in some patients, together with a retrognathic jaw and deviated septum.[4]

Wikipedia's palatal expansion article says expansion usually opens a gap between the upper front teeth, that treatment after the growth spurt mainly tips back teeth rather than widening bone, and that studies reported roughly one third to one half of expansion lost before stabilising.[15] It also notes posterior and nasal-aperture expansion are described as important in treating obstructive sleep apnea.[15]

No published study ranks palate width against other facial features for attractiveness, and orthodontic research on expansion concentrates on arch width, crossbite and airway outcomes rather than on perceived facial appearance.

Expansion appliances can cause speech changes such as lisps, extra saliva, headaches, tongue sores and gaps between front teeth. Bone changes such as buccal fenestration and extrusion of back teeth have been described, and adult techniques add mini-implant or surgical risks.[15] Orthodontists and oral surgeons assess whether a true transverse deficiency exists before treating.[3]

Narrow palate threads on looksmax.org range from questions about whether a particular palate counts as narrow to comparisons of famous people. Titles include threads claiming that the bodybuilder Zyzz had a very narrow palate and that someone named Ramirez did.[16][17] A thread titled 'narrow palate vs wide palate' compares the two, and others ask whether a narrow palate matters at all.[2][18]

The recurring point of dispute is whether palate width is a primary driver of facial attractiveness or a secondary feature. Posters in one thread say many male models have narrow palates and that tooth shape, color and gum show matter more, while a reply argues it still improves attractiveness.[2]

No clinical studies have tested the narrow palate theory itself, meaning whether palate width predicts facial attractiveness or whether expansion improves it. Studies of palatal expansion in orthodontic populations measure arch width, crossbite correction and airway outcomes, and are summarised in reviews.[3] A meta-analysis of pacifier use examined the debated link between non-nutritive sucking and a high narrow palate.[13]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org the narrow palate is treated as part of the maxilla and midface discussion, with threads on identification, expansion options and whether it matters.[1] Members debate identification, expansion options and whether palate width matters at all.[2][10] Members debate identification, expansion options and whether palate width matters at all.[2][10]
